Entries.Text: Toggle the display of the Control instructions in the top-left corner.
Toggle the display of the Profiling information in the top-left corner.
Toggle the display of the current Translation Increment in the top-left corner.
Toggle the display of the current Rotation Increment in the top-left corner.
Toggle the display of the viewport tooltip on hover.
Toggle the display of the placement orb within the viewport.
Toggle the display of the compass within the viewport.
Set the minimum distance at which entities will be rendered within the viewport.
Set the maximum distance at which entities will be rendered within the viewport.
Set the field of view used by the camera.
Mouse sensitivty for turning the camera.
Set the speed at which the camera will move when the Left or Right Shift key is pressed whilst moving.
Set the speed at which the camera will move whilst moving normally.
Set the speed at which the camera will move when the Left or Right Control key is pressed whilst moving.
Set the minimum distance at which entities will be rendered within the viewport.
Set the maximum distance at which entities will be rendered within the viewport.
The sensitivity of the mouse panning.
Set the height of the view in world units.
Set the angle of the view.
Set the scaling of the view.
If enabled, materials that animate over time will play in the viewport. If disabled, they hold their current frame.
How strongly vegetation moves in the viewport. The game's own wind varies by place, so this is an approximation of it.
The direction vegetation is blown in, in degrees.
Flags, cloth and creatures with baked vertex animations play them.
Hanging objects and leaves sway back and forth.
Flocks of birds flap and fly around their paths.
Materials blend their texture layers. If disabled, only the first layer is shown.
Materials apply their detail albedo and overlay normal textures.
Magma materials give off their flowing glow.
Materials give off light from their emissive textures.
Sky, clouds and flames are drawn unlit. This stands in for the game's shaders, which rely on its scene.
Water gets moving ripples and a smooth surface. This stands in for the game's shaders, which rely on its scene.
Fur is cut out into strands instead of being drawn as solid cards.
Light models inside environment boxes with the map's baked irradiance volumes, instead of the environment map. Outside every box, models keep the environment map's light.
The volumes' light is in the game's own units. Auto exposure scales it so the volumes' average matches the viewport's default ambient light. Current exposure: {0:F1}
Multiplies the volumes' light. With Auto Exposure off this is the exposure itself; around 25 matches typical maps.

The bake of the irradiance volumes to light the maps with, the NN of the map's envmap_NN files. Bakes are probably times of day; most Nightreign maps only have bake 0. A change applies the next time a map is loaded.

Blend the volumes' light towards a second bake, as the game does between times of day. The second bake's textures load with the map, so switching this on or changing the bake applies the next time a map is loaded.
The bake to blend towards. Volumes that don't have it keep the first bake's light.
How far towards the second bake: 0 is the first bake, 1 the second. Applies at once.

Scale the environment map's reflections by how bright the volumes' light is at each point compared with the volume's average, as the game does, so reflections darken in shadow and brighten in lit areas.

Take the sun's direction, color and intensity, the hemisphere ambient light, and the exposure from the map's GPARAMs, as the game does. The irradiance volumes then take the same exposure instead of their auto exposure, and the hemisphere replaces the grey environment map for ambient light and reflections. With several maps loaded, the first by name with its own GPARAM lights them all.

Multiplies the GPARAM's exposure. Most maps switch on the game's auto exposure, which adjusts the exposure to what is on screen; Smithbox uses the GPARAM's value as it is, so some maps may look too bright or too dark.

The GPARAM's hemisphere light (sky color from above, ground color from below) lights what the irradiance volumes don't cover, and the reflections. With this on it also adds to the volumes' light, which matches the game.
Light DS3's map pieces with their lightmaps (the DOL textures of gi_env), as the game does, in place of the light probes. Applies to maps loaded after it is changed.
The viewport's scale on the lightmaps' light. How the game scales them isn't known, so match the map pieces against the game (or against the light-probe-lit objects beside them) and report the value.

Draws a part of the map lighting in place of the lit image. Source: where each surface's light from around comes from, green a lightmap, blue light probes or irradiance volumes, red the hemisphere, yellow a lightmapped material whose part found no lightmap. Ambient: that light alone, without the surface's color. Sun Mask: how much of the sun each surface lets through, white all, black none.
Light with {0}, the GPARAM the selected collision's scene GPARAM picks (its sub ID N picks mAA_BB_0N00), as the game does while the player is on it.
Select a collision whose scene GPARAM sub ID has a file in its area, to light with that GPARAM.

Light with a weather, by its GparamId in WeatherParam: the area's own version of the GPARAM (mAA_BB_CCWW) where there is one, and the shared outdoor overlays m00_00_WWWW_weatheroutdoor and _weatherbase over it, which are what rain and snow change.

Read the weather's shared overlays (m00_00_WWWW_weatheroutdoor, then _weatherbase) before the map's own GPARAM, as the game does outdoors. Their light, tone map, fog and Wet values replace the map's. Switch off for an interior.
Time {0}: the GPARAMs' key for this timezone. In Elden Ring it is also the time irradiance volume bake {1} was made at.
Irradiance Volumes Follow the Time of Day

Light with the irradiance volume bakes of the time of day, blending between the two timezones either side of it, as the game does: bake N is timezone N. Every bake is loaded with the map, so the time can be changed without waiting; maps loaded before this was switched on load their other bakes as the time reaches them.
The bakes follow the time of day (Map Lighting): bake {0} towards {1} by {2:0.##}.
Light Characters with the Model Set

Light characters (c####) with the GPARAM LightSet's model set (ID {0}) instead of the scene's: its own sun, the fill lights (Light 1, which can turn with the camera, and the local lights) and its hemisphere. Not yet compared with the game, so it is off by default.
Fill the viewport's background with the BG color of the map's GPARAM (Setting Info), at the GPARAM's exposure, instead of the background color of the settings.
No loaded map has its own GPARAM, so the viewport's own sun is used.
The sun comes from the map's GPARAMs (the Map Lighting tab).
Light with the Lights Near the Camera
Light the viewports with the loaded maps' BTL lights near the camera, nearest first. When off, only selected lights shine. Selected lights always shine, wherever they are.
How far from the camera a light can be and still shine.
Also only light with a light within its own EnableDist of the camera, as the game turns it on. An EnableDist of 0 is taken as no limit.
The most lights shaded at once, the nearest kept. Every pixel checks each of them, so lower this if the viewport slows down.
Not used while the map's GPARAMs light the viewport: the lights' power is in the game's units, so it takes the GPARAM's exposure ({0:0.###}), as the sun does.
Lighting with {0} of the {1} lights in range.
Not used while the map's GPARAMs light the viewport: the volumes take the GPARAM's exposure, as the sun does.

The GPARAM each value is looked for in first. Values it doesn't have come from mapbase, then default.
Any of the project's GPARAMs can be chosen: one from another area lights every loaded map.
The time on the GPARAMs' TimeOfDay scale. Elden Ring keys its lighting at 0, 4, 8, 12, 15, 21 and 22.5, where 0 is morning, 12 evening and 15 night.
Volumes in the shading table: {0} of {1}
The linked environment boxes whose four textures of the bake are on the GPU. Boxes the game skips are left out.
{0}: {1} volumes in bake {2}, {3} of {4} environment boxes linked
Environment boxes without a volume: {0}, skipped by the game: {1}
Open the Irradiance Volumes tab of the Validation tools, which lists each environment box's volume and can fill their volume ID property from their names.

Hold Ctrl while dragging the gizmo to snap.

Rotation snaps to steps of this many degrees (0 to disable). Translation snaps to the squares of the grid shown in the Grid Configuration tool, while that grid is visible.
Set the gizmo to Translation mode.
Set the gizmo to Rotation mode.
Set the gizmo to Scale mode.
Place the gizmo origin based on the selection's local position.
Place the gizmo origin based on the selection's world position.
Orient the gizmo origin based on the world position.
Orient the gizmo origin based on the bounding box.
Whether to render objects in the viewport.
Whether to render textures in the viewport.
Draws surfaces fullbright, with their textures unlit. Map lighting, global illumination, shadows, fog and post effects are turned off, whatever the Rendering tool says.
Lights the scene as the game does. Map lighting, global illumination, shadows, fog and post effects follow the settings in the Rendering tool.
Shows the surfaces' normals in place of the image: the Normals surface view.
Whether to cull objects in the viewport outside of the camera frustum.
Whether models are lit by the baked irradiance volumes. When off, they take the ambient light outside the volumes instead. The same switch as the Global Illumination tab of the Rendering tool.

Whether the viewports are lit by the map's GPARAM lighting: its sun, hemisphere, exposure, tone map and background. When off, the Scene Lighting tab's own sun and settings are used. The same switch as the Map Lighting tab of the Rendering tool.
Whether the sun casts shadows. When off, the shadow maps aren't drawn. The same switch as the Shadows tab of the Rendering tool.
Whether to attempt to hide model masks based on entity NpcParam flags.
Determines the distance in front of the camera the placement orb is.
Determines the size of the compass.
Determines the angle offset when determining which direction is north.
Determines the radius of the dummy polygon mesh.
Determines the radius of the node mesh.
Determines the size of the dummy polygon ID and bone name text in the viewport.
Toggle which models are loaded during a map load.
Toggle which textures are loaded during a map load.

Holding click on the viewport will enable camera controls.
Use WASD to navigate.
Use right click to rotate the camera.
Hold Shift to temporarily speed up and Ctrl to temporarily slow down.
Scroll the mouse wheel to adjust overall speed.
Hold Ctrl, Alt and left click to make a box selection.

Holding click on the viewport will enable camera controls.
Pan the screen with the middle mouse button.
Use right click to rotate the camera.
Hold right click and scroll the mouse wheel to adjust the zoom.
Hold Ctrl, Alt and left click to make a box selection.

How the viewport's HDR scene is brought down to the screen. From GPARAM uses the map's Tone Map group under map lighting: ToneMapMode 8, which every Elden Ring GPARAM uses, is a Reinhard curve whose white point is the Reinhard Contrast times the Reinhard White Balance, and 7 is the filmic curve. This is an approximation of the game's curves, and anything without map lighting is clipped. Clamp clips at white, as the viewport did before it had an HDR target.
Multiplies the scene before the curve. The GPARAM's exposure is already applied to the map's lighting, so this is on top of it.
The brightness that the Reinhard curve takes to white, when the curve is set to Reinhard. From GPARAM uses the map's own.

Shadows cast by the sun, in up to four cascades. Under map lighting the cascade splits, the far fade and the bias come from the map's GPARAM Shadows group; otherwise from Elden Ring's mapbase. Only models drawn with the full material shader cast and receive them.
The size of each cascade's shadow map. The four cascades share one map twice this size on each side, for each viewport.
How much of the sun a shadow takes away: 1 for all of it.
Multiplies the GPARAM's Depth Bias and Slope Scaled Depth Bias. Raise it if surfaces shade themselves in stripes, lower it if shadows come away from what casts them.

Whether parts cast shadows as their IsShadowSrc or IsShadowOnly says, and receive them as their IsShadowDest says (ShadowSource and ShadowDest in DS3 and Bloodborne; in Elden Ring the Is Sun Shadow Source, Is Shadow Only and Is Shadow Destination flags, each only when its override is on). Otherwise every part does both. Applies to parts as they are loaded or edited, so reload the map to apply it to all of them.
The map whose GPARAM lighting and irradiance bake light this editor's viewports, as it has no map of its own. Lit with: {0}. Shared by the Model and Time Act Editors.
The project has no map to borrow lighting from.
The irradiance volume of the map's bake to light with. Automatic takes the one whose average light is the median of the map's, among those with the most bakes.

The size of the box the volume is stretched over, centred on the origin. The volume's own box isn't read, so this isn't the game's scale; a smaller box shows more of the volume's variation across the model.
The map has no irradiance volumes.

Draws the screen effects of the map's GPARAMs between the scene and the tone map: bloom, fog, light shafts and others, each with a switch of its own once it is drawn. Off: the scene goes straight to the tone map.
No screen effects are drawn. They need the map's lighting (Map Lighting tab), and FXAA its switch.

Where the GPARAM's Tone Map switches auto exposure on, adjusts the exposure to what is on screen: by Middle Gray minus the scene's mean log2 light, within Adaption Min to Max, at the adapt speeds. Off: the GPARAM's Exposure as it is.
Auto exposure: scene mean {0} (log2), adjusted {1} EV towards {2}
The scene's mean is in the game's light units, before any exposure. If the image looks too dark or bright against the game, report these numbers with the map and time.
Where the GPARAM's Bloom group is on, blurs what is brighter than Glare Threshold over Glare Num Levels levels and adds it at Bloom Alpha.

Smooths jagged edges after the tone map, with the GPARAM Anti-Alias group's FXAA values (Elden Ring's mapbase without map lighting). Used for every Anti-Alias Type but TAA's (5), and for that too when TAA is off.

Where the GPARAM Anti-Alias group's type is TAA (5, Elden Ring's mapbase), the scene is drawn a sub-pixel off each frame over JitterCount frames and blended into a history, by Feedback Weight, less with depth, and sharpened by Sharpen Intensity. Smooths edges, grass and SSAO/SSR noise while the camera is still; replaces FXAA.

Where the GPARAM's VolumetricFog group is on, hazes the scene with its height fog out to Far Depth (and to Fog End Depth with Enable Analytical Fog), lit by the Sky Light and Dir Light colors. Needs map lighting.

Transparent flvers (water, glass, foliage cards) fog themselves at their own depth with the same fog, as they are drawn over the fogged scene. Alpha blended ones get the fog's light too; additive ones are only dimmed.
Shades the fog's sunlight with the sun's shadow maps, which gives shafts of shadow through gaps. Needs Shadows on.

In a weather whose WeatherParam wets things (Wet Time above 0), surfaces facing the sky darken towards the GPARAM Wet group's Override Albedo and turn glossier towards Override Shininess, by Albedo Rate and Shininess Rate; walls half as much. Needs a weather and Outdoor Weather.

Keeps surfaces under roofs, arches and tree canopies dry, from a depth map of the scene seen straight down over 256 m round the camera. It is drawn again when the camera moves 32 m or the map's models change. Past the square, everything facing the sky is wet.
Rain mask: round x {0}, z {1}, drawn {2} times
Where the map of what the rain reaches was last drawn round. The count should only go up as the camera moves 32 m or models load, not every frame.

Where the GPARAM's LightShaft group is on, rays fan out from the sun where the sky shows round it, colored by Sky Multiply Color and Sky Add Color, whose intensity (w) is 0 at many times of day. Needs map lighting.

Shows what the screen space effects read in place of the image: the normals, roughness and specular of opaque flvers as they are, or the indirect diffuse light, tone mapped. Pixels no flver drew are dark grey.

Where the GPARAM's Glow Filter is on (Elden Ring's mapbase, so every map), what surfaces give off themselves (emissive textures, magma) is blurred over Glow NumLevels levels and added round them, however bright the scene is. Only opaque models glow. Needs map lighting.
The viewport's own scale on the glow, on top of the GPARAM's Blur RgbScale. 1 is the GPARAM as read.

The viewport's own scale on the bloom, on top of the GPARAM's GlareBloom Alpha and the game's own scale (Sekiro 0.5, matched against the game). 1 is the game as matched. The game sets part of its bloom's strength in its code, which isn't known, so if a game's bloom looks too strong or weak, set this to match and report the value.

The viewport's own scale on the fog's density, on top of the GPARAM's (already divided by its GameScale, which Sekiro sets to 1-12) and the game's own scale (Sekiro 0.1, matched against the game). 1 is the game as matched. If a game's fog looks too thick or thin, set this to match and report the value, with the time of day and the game scale the Post Effects table shows.

Where the GPARAM's SSR group is on, glossy surfaces reflect what is on screen in place of the environment's reflection, with its reject thresholds, ray steps and fades (Elden Ring's maps all take mapbase's). Where a ray finds nothing, the environment's reflection stays. Water and glass, which are transparent, aren't reflective yet. Runs with or without map lighting.
How much of the environment's reflection SSR replaces where its rays hit: 1 all of it, as read from the GPARAM, 0 none.

Darkens the ambient light in creases and where surfaces meet, with the GPARAM SSAO group's values (Elden Ring's maps all take mapbase's). Only the indirect light is taken away, so sunlit faces keep their sun. Runs with or without map lighting.
The viewport's own scale on how much SSAO darkens, on top of the GPARAM's AO Scale and AO Offset. 1 is the GPARAM as read.
Adds the map's lights near the camera to the fog, by Local Light Scale, over their range times Local Light Dist Scale.
middle gray {0}, adapting {1} to {2} EV at {3} / {4}
{0} levels, final scale {1}, RGB scale {2}, alpha scale {3}
from {0}, sky mask {1} rad, blur {2} x {3}
density {0} + {1} x exp(-{2} x (y - {3})), levelling off at 2 x {1} below {3}; over game scale {5}; scattering g {4}
scale {0}, offset {1}, kernel {2} to {3} px, fading from {4} m
shininess over {0}, fresnel over {1}, fade to viewer {2}

Where the GPARAM's ColorGrading group is on, the image goes through the LUT its LutSourceId names, from the maps' mAA_cgrading textures, blending between the two LUTs either side of the time of day. Needs map lighting.
Puts the clipping distances, field of view, sensitivity, move speeds, pan sensitivity, orthographic size and oblique settings back to their defaults.
How fast the camera turns and moves.
Switch to Game render mode to change these:
Opens the Viewport Rendering section of the tool window, which has every lighting, shadow, post effect and material setting.
The direction the sun shines in.
Multiplies the direct light: the sun and the other lights.
Multiplies the indirect light: the ambient and environment light.
Multiplies the brightness of the whole scene.
A point light that follows the camera, for seeing into dark interiors.
How many grass blades are drawn. Changing it rebuilds the grass, so it applies when the slider is let go.
Editor render mode switches off everything but layer blending, the shader types, grass and collision opacity. Switch to Game mode to change the rest.
What the viewport is drawing right now. Click the eye to show or hide this section in every tab.
Per loaded map, the values its GPARAMs give and the file each comes from. Click the eye to show or hide this section in every tab.
Debug views. Click the eye to show or hide this section in every tab. It is always shown while a debug view is on.
How the maps' GPARAM lighting is used.
Which GPARAM file and weather the lighting is read from.
Which map and irradiance volume the lighting is borrowed from.
The hour the GPARAMs are read at.
The viewport's own sun, used when map lighting doesn't give one.
Scales applied on top of the light the scene is given.
A light that follows the camera.
How the irradiance volumes light the scene.
Which of the volumes' bakes is used, and whether two are blended.
Whether the loaded maps' EnvMapEffectBoxes are linked to a volume.
Which of the loaded maps' BTL lights are used.
How bright the BTL lights are.
How the HDR scene is brought down to the screen.
The screen effects the maps' GPARAMs ask for.
Exposure, bloom, glow and color grading.
Wetness, ambient occlusion and screen space reflections.
The material and vertex animation the shaders play.
The material features drawn on surfaces.
The special shaders some materials use.
The wind the swaying materials follow.
How grass and collisions are drawn.

The Gparam Editor lights its map with the GPARAM selected in its file list, including unsaved edits. Pick the map in the Viewport Preview section. The weather and time of day are the Map Editor's, so both editors light a map alike.
Following the selected value's time of day: {0}.
Show the active map (the map the content tree shows and new objects go into) in the viewport overlay.
